Luxury Japanese food in Ho Chi Minh
Mar 2024 • Business
This high-end Japanese restaurant is located one alley away from Le Thanh Ton Street. This time, we used it for a social gathering with a Japanese expatriate client. On the first floor, there is a kitchen and counter seats on the right side, and on the second floor, there are private rooms with sunken kotatsu tables. We toasted with Black Label draft beer, ordered a course meal, and had sake such as Kaga Tobi and Kenbishi, and shochu such as Akagiri. We had egg tofu topped with salmon roe, sashimi such as medium fatty tuna, sea bream, and squid, roast beef and fried puffer fish, shrimp baguette toast, tuna nigiri and scallop nigiri, tekkamaki and dried gourd rolls, and ice cream for dessert, all accompanied by sake and shochu. It was a very delicious high-end Japanese meal in Ho Chi Minh City.

Great and Varied Japanese Fare
Feb 2018 • Couples
This place offers a great display kitchen, where you can watch with anticipation, the steps taken to create some delicious food. Tempura was light, crispy and under the fried exterior offered fresh and tasty bits of vegetables and shrimp. The dipping sauce had a spike of fest ginger. Noodles are prepped in a side room. Another craft touch to this modern Japanese eatery. Fish was fresh, oily and have high quality. Noodles and broth were stellar. Sake selection was good and real imported Sapporo not the swill sold under the Sapporo name you typically see here. I'll be back again and again.

The location is perfect inside Japan town, expensive decor in a very large building with plenty of private rooms. We had dinner at the counter. All chefs are Vietnamese but well trained. Stumbled on this gem
May 2017 • Couples
My husband and I kept walking by Syunkato and finally stopped in and were not disappointed. We ordered the omakase. It was beautiful and so delicious. We saw as few other items being made and ordered those as well, each was more delicious than the last.

Word to those who don't speak Vietnamese or Japanese. Sit at the sushi bar so you can see what is being made and point it out, no one really speaks English. District 1 is known for tourists and Japanese expats, this place is some of the best sushi we've had, including Hong Kong and most 5 star places in NY or LA.

Go, sit and the bar, and eat what looks the best!!! You will not be disapppointed!

Horrendous Service Marred Good Food
Dec 2014 • Friends
I went back to Syunkato last night with a friend. This is my fifth time. So what changed? The food hasn't. Still one of the best in Saigon as far as sushi is concerned. 

The thing that really killed it for me was their service. 

1. Language/Communication. Granted I do not expect them to speak English here. All the friends I brought with me are either local or speak very fluent Vietnamese. Their inability to communicate in any language (except for Japanese perhaps) is confounding. 

2. Service. Very exclusive to Japanese customers. I felt like I'm eating there for free rather than paying customer.

It's not like it just happened. The first couple times I tried to be understanding. But it's just consistently bad in term of communication and service.

I noticed that the best looking food are usually not on the menu (but cooked behind the counter). Just like last time, I asked if we can order the same thing pointing to what the Japanese chef is cooking. 

Just like last time, the waiter said "no." With no explanation whatsoever. This time I asked them to explain, in Vietnamese. The answer was completely incoherent. "We cannot because it's for other customer." What?!?

I whipped out Tripadvisor and noticed another review in Japanese with 1 star. I Google translated it. Lo and behold, the review talked basically spoke about the horrendous service here, lacking heart.

Now I completely regret being the first person to put them on Tripadvisor. I need to write this follow-up review and give them Terrible grade (to offset my Excelllent grade).

Syunkato just have this arrogance about them because they have good food and steady stream of Japanese expats client. Good on them. They can continue to cater exclusively to these Japanese crowd. I'll take my money elsewhere.

Fortunately, I'd discovered other great Japanese sushi in Saigon. At Inaho, I can have equally good sushi with great service to match. I will write my review on Inaho (although I'm glad to see they already have pretty high mark). So if you're looking for food that's as good as Syunkato, at slightly lower price but way better service, go for Inaho (just a walking distance from here BTW).

The best sushi I've had in Saigon so far...
Aug 2014 • Friends
I stumbled onto Syunkato by accident when I was exploring the restaurants in the Le Than Ton area on my second trip to Saigon last year. Japanese restaurants lined the whole Ngo Van Nam street, an offshoot of Le Than Ton (Little Tokyo part of it). 

What struck me about the place is the lack of sign and consistent number of Japanese-only clientele walking in-and-out. I peaked in the saw a typically well designed sushi bar.

Menu is almost completely in Japanese-only.

You have to be pretty darn confident (or completely foolish) about your food to take this approach. See Jiro's and many similar highly acclaimed sushi joints with Tokyo; small, zero marketing, always full, insider's knowledge, could careless about catering to non-Japanese. Mental note to try. 

8 trips later and here I am. By then, I'd tried some of the best such as Ichiban and Le Phum (spelling?) (I'm leaving out Sushi Bar chains as they're not even worth a mention) in town.

We tried beef tongue, sushi platter, shrimp tempura, and sashimi platter (not on the menu). I was surprised by the freshness of the fish, especially on the ones used in the sashimi platter.

Service will be a bit tougher if you don't speak Vietnamese or Japanese as those are the only languages spoke proficiently there. That could be a challenge/drawback to some. My friend spoke some Vietnamese and I spoke smatter of Japanese. Enough to get by and get us what we wanted.

Unfortunately, there was slight hiccup in the order despite communicating in Vietnamese our preference. The whole thing came out to 1.5 million VND (or about $75 USD) for 2 person for orders I mentioned. 

I spent less at Ichiban (where sushi is not as fresh) and more at Le Pham. However, I know this would be my goto place unless I find something better (although Ichiban is friendlier/more homely and good for sushi craving on a budget).

Bottomline, Syunkato is THE best sushi restaurant I'd tried in Vietnam so far.
